Wave-Corrected Caustics over Photon Splatting: A Comparative Evaluation against Photon Mapping and Path Tracing

Debyte · D:/ValueProjects/caustics · Draft, 2026-10-12

Abstract

Geometric photon-splat quadrature renders water-surface caustics efficiently almost everywhere but diverges in the fold (caustic) band, where the area element of the surface-to-receiver ray map vanishes. We present a hybrid estimator in which the geometric quadrature is the backbone and a wave correction is applied only inside a narrowly detected fold band: the band's geometric energy is redistributed according to the Airy fold profile \(|Ai(-s/w)|^2\), with a per-channel fringe width \(w\) scaling as \(\lambda^{2/3}\). We then ask the question that decides whether such a method is worth using, and answer it computationally against the caustic solvers in current practice — PBRT-v4 SPPM, Blender Cycles, and Mitsuba 3.

Against an independent brute-force geometric ground truth (810 k explicit rays, no parametrisation, no Jacobian, no renormalisation), ours scores \(0.917\) at 40 mm tiles against \(0.853\) for SPPM and \(0.828\) for Cycles, and at 5 mm tiles \(0.721\) / \(0.722\) / \(0.405\): we lead at every scale and SPPM ties us only at the finest. Cycles covers 54.7% of the ground truth's caustic core against our 99.9%. On the reference conforming solver the converged two-dimensional shape agrees at \(r = +0.932\). Transport throughput is 96.41% at three wavelengths with Fresnel reflection as the only loss, though the baked field holds 0.28 of the geometric energy because the display ceiling and the Airy replacement shed it by construction.

On speed the result is a difference of cost structure, not a uniform win. Producing a caustic takes 36.22 ms at \(512^2\) against SPPM's 34 s — a factor near 1000 — and the bake is deterministic, so a re-baked animated sequence costs 0.34 s per frame rather than a fresh convergence: on an identical 120-frame orbit clip we finish in 773.3 s against Cycles' 1043.2 s while flickering 7.9× less in the caustic region. But Cycles is marginally ahead on the static-camera clip (453.0 s against 481.9 s including bake), the two are within noise on a single production still at 2048 spp, plain Monte-Carlo is more accurate than ours below ~262 k splats, and our advantage is amortised against one fixed geometry family.

The wave physics is verified independently of the solver: the profile table matches true Airy to \(8.1\times10^{-3}\) of peak, the canonical cubic-phase fold integral peaks at \(X=-1.00\) where \(Ai^2\) predicts \(-1.0188\), and the fringe scales as \(\lambda^{0.6977}\) against an analytic \(\lambda^{2/3}\). Three claims from our own earlier record are withdrawn. Laboratory validation is out of scope and no claim here depends on it.

Keywords: caustics, wave optics, Airy function, fold catastrophe, photon splatting, photon mapping, SPPM, rendering, comparative evaluation.

1. Introduction

A refracting water surface concentrates sunlight into a caustic. The standard fast estimator for this is photon splatting: sample the surface, refract by Snell's law, follow each ray to the receiver, and accumulate. It is cheap because the ray map is smooth almost everywhere. Its failure is local and fatal in the place that matters: where the map folds, the Jacobian determinant vanishes and the geometric density diverges as \(|\det J|^{-1}\), so any discretisation either blows the display range or must be clamped away.

Production renderers do not solve this cleanly either, for a different reason. A path tracer must hit a small, bright, thin feature by chance; the caustic is exactly the rarity that makes the estimator slow, and in our measurements Cycles' caustic error does not improve with sample count in this scene. The solvers that do converge it — photon mapping and its progressive variants — spend samples per shot on an estimate that has to be recomputed whenever anything changes.

This paper contributes a fold-local wave correction and, more importantly for practice, an honest comparative evaluation of it. We take the position that a caustic method earns its place by being faster, cleaner, or better converged than what is already in use, on the workloads people render. The paper is therefore organised around questions that can be settled computationally:

  1. Is the caustic right? Measured against an independent brute-force geometric trace that neither method produced, against a closed-form caustic of a solid refracting cylinder, and against the converged shape from the reference photon-mapping solver.
  2. Is it cheap? Measured as bake cost and as end-to-end animated-clip cost, at matched camera paths, geometry, wave phase and sample counts.
  3. Where does it lose? Stated explicitly, including every configuration in which a competing method is ahead.

Scope, stated once and applying to every number. One scene: a 6 × 6 m water patch, depth 1 m, four directional sine waves, sun direction \((-0.35,-0.25,-1)\), \(t\) = 1.7 s, airy_scale = 0.02 m unless stated. One machine: i7-14650HX, 16C/24T, RTX 4060 Laptop. One scene family for the showcase geometry: a cylindrical glass of radius 35 mm, height 90 mm, wall 3.5 mm, filled to 59.4 mm. There is no laboratory ground truth here, by design — physical-apparatus validation is out of scope for this work and no claim depends on it. Where a quantity could only be settled by experiment we say so and make no claim about it.

2. Related work and the novelty gap

Geometric caustics — solved, sparsely shipped. Photon mapping [Jensen 1996, 2001] is the classic specular–diffuse–specular caustic solver, shipped in LuxCoreRender and in limited form in Blender Cycles as light tracing / photon path. It is absent from Mitsuba 3's main integrators and from PBRT-v4's main CPU integrators, though PBRT-v4 ships SPPM [Hachisuka et al. 2008] plus BDPT and MLT. Progressive and stochastic PPM variants remain largely research code and LuxCore. Manifold Next Event Estimation [Hanika et al. 2015] exists as a Cycles toggle but not in Mitsuba 3 or PBRT-v4 mainline. Specular Manifold Sampling [Zeltner et al. 2020] and its bisection variant [2022], Manifold Path Guiding [2023] and general path guiding [Müller et al. 2017, shipped in Cycles] are research-only or not themselves caustic solvers. The situation is that geometric caustics are well understood and only partially shipped.

Wave optics in graphics — largely unshipped. Yan et al. [2018] model microgeometry scratches as phase gratings for stable glints; no shipping renderer implements it. The closest shipped wave features are analytic thin-film interference (Cycles' thin-film toggle, Mitsuba 3's principledthin BSDF), which are not general diffraction. Bar et al. [2019] treat Monte-Carlo speckle in scattering media; a 2023 generalised ray formulation for wave-optics rendering remains research-only. UTD/PTD edge diffraction [Kouyoumjian & Pathak 1974] is standard in acoustics and RF planning but absent from major graphics path tracers. Frosted and Airy-fringe caustics remain research-only.

Physics root and the exact gap. Berry & Upstill [1980] is the canonical treatment of catastrophe optics and the Airy fold. A title search for wave-optics caustic rendering returns physics papers, not renderers: no production or research renderer ships Airy- (fold) or Pearcey- (cusp) regularised caustics. This work occupies that gap by construction — not with a global wave solve, but with a band-local replacement of the geometric singularity, gated by the analytic fold locus and flux-conserved inside the band. The three measured methodological rules of Section 6.5 are, to our knowledge, not previously documented as a design discipline for wave-corrected caustics.

Caveat carried forward: the prior-art survey hit HTTP 429 on arXiv and Semantic Scholar; versioned citation identifiers must be re-verified from a keyed connection before submission.

3. Theory and formulation

3.1 Geometric backbone and the ray map

Let the water surface be a height field \(h(\mathbf{x}, t)\) over \(\mathbf{x} = (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2\), a superposition of directional sinusoids,

\[h(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_{i=1}^{4} A_i \sin\!\big(k_i\,(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}) - \omega_i t\big), \qquad k_i = \frac{2\pi}{\Lambda_i},\]

with amplitudes \(A_i = \{0.65, 0.40, 0.25, 0.15\}\) mm at wavelengths \(\Lambda_i = \{42, 27, 17, 11\}\) mm. The outward surface normal follows from the analytic gradient,

\[\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{(-\partial_x h,\; -\partial_y h,\; 1)}{\sqrt{1 + |\nabla h|^2}}.\]

A distant source with unit direction \(\hat{\mathbf{s}}\) (pointing along propagation, downward) refracts into the water by Snell's law in vector form. With \(\eta = n_1/n_2\) and \(c_i = -\hat{\mathbf{s}}\cdot\mathbf{n} > 0\),

\[\hat{\mathbf{t}} = \eta\,\hat{\mathbf{s}} + \big(\eta\,c_i - \sqrt{1 - \eta^2(1-c_i^2)}\big)\,\mathbf{n}, \qquad \eta^2(1-c_i^2) \le 1 \ \text{(else TIR)}. \tag{1}\]

The refracted ray reaches the receiver plane \(z = -D\) after a path length \(s = (-D - h(\mathbf{x}))/\hat t_z\), giving the surface-to-receiver ray map

\[\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \hat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{x})\,\frac{-D - h(\mathbf{x})}{\hat t_z(\mathbf{x})}, \qquad \mathbf{H} : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2. \tag{2}\]

Splatting assigns each surface cell an energy proportional to its area, so the irradiance on the receiver is the push-forward

\[I(\mathbf{u}) = \sum_{\mathbf{x}:\,\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{u}} \frac{1}{|\det J_{\mathbf{H}}(\mathbf{x})|}, \qquad J_{\mathbf{H}} = \begin{pmatrix} \partial H_x/\partial x & \partial H_x/\partial y \\[2pt] \partial H_y/\partial x & \partial H_y/\partial y \end{pmatrix}. \tag{3}\]

This is the entire method's structure: the \(|\det J_{\mathbf{H}}|^{-1}\) factor is what makes photon splatting efficient where the map is smooth and what makes it diverge where it is not.

3.2 The fold and the failure of the geometric model

The fold (caustic) locus is the set where the map is degenerate,

\[\mathcal{F} = \{\, \mathbf{x} \;:\; \det J_{\mathbf{H}}(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \,\}. \tag{4}\]

Because (3) evaluates to \(1/0\) there, geometric quadrature cannot represent the neighbourhood of \(\mathcal{F}\) at any resolution: refining the grid moves samples around inside a diverging integrand rather than converging. This is a property of the model, not of its discretisation, and it is the reason a wave treatment is needed rather than a better sampler.

Detecting \(\mathcal{F}\) matters as much as correcting it. A detector that flags "the brightest 2% of pixels" always returns exactly 2% of the image regardless of the true fold fraction, so it cannot converge under refinement. We instead threshold the analytic \(|\det J_{\mathbf{H}}|\) computed by finite differences of \(\mathbf{H}\) (2), at the second percentile; Section 6.5 reports the measured convergence difference.

3.3 The Airy fold profile

Near a fold the wave-optical amplitude is given by the canonical fold diffraction integral: a wavefront with cubic phase, integrated over the pupil \(\rho \in [-1,1]\),

\[U(x) = \int_{-1}^{1} \exp\!\Big( i\, \tfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\big[\, \tfrac{c\,\rho^3}{6} + \rho\, x \,\big]\Big)\, d\rho, \qquad I(x) = |U(x)|^2. \tag{5}\]

Substituting \(\rho = \alpha s\) and matching the cubic term to \(s^3/3\) gives \(\alpha = (2/(kc))^{1/3}\) with \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\), so the canonical coordinate is

\[X = x\,k^{2/3}\,2^{1/3}\,c^{-1/3}, \qquad I(x) \;\propto\; \big|Ai(-X)\big|^2, \tag{6}\]

the squared Airy function [Airy 1838; Berry & Upstill 1980]. Equation (6) is the object we substitute for the geometric divergence inside the band: it is finite everywhere, peaks at \(X = -1.0188\), and has the Fresnel-like oscillatory tail on the bright side that a geometric model cannot produce.

The practical form used by the implementation is a normalised profile in the signed distance \(s\) to the locus, with a per-channel width \(w\),

\[P(s;w) = \big|Ai(-s/w)\big|^2 \Big/ \max_u |Ai(-u)|^2, \qquad b(s) = 0.15 + 0.85\,P(s;w), \tag{7}\]

evaluated through a 2048-entry table over \(u \in [0,8]\) with linear interpolation; the \(0.15\) floor keeps the band's skirt continuous with the geometric field outside it.

3.4 Why the fringe width scales as \(\lambda^{2/3}\)

Equation (5) contains one wavelength and one geometric quantity, the cubic coefficient \(c\) of the wavefront. Dimensional analysis of the canonical mapping gives the fold's spatial scale directly:

\[d(\lambda, c) = k^{-2/3}\,2^{-1/3}\,c^{1/3} \;\propto\; \lambda^{2/3}. \tag{8}\]

So the fringe spacing is not linear in \(\lambda\) and not the Fresnel \(\sqrt{\lambda}\) law: it is the two-thirds power, and it follows from the geometry of the fold rather than being fitted. The implementation therefore sets

\[w_c = w_{\text{ref}}\Big(\frac{\lambda_c}{550\,\text{nm}}\Big)^{2/3}, \tag{9}\]

per channel \(c \in \{650, 550, 450\}\) nm. Section 6.4 verifies both the profile (7) and the exponent (8) numerically against independent computations; the exponent is the load-bearing number for the entire dispersion story, because chromatic separation in this model is carried by \(w_c\) and by the per-channel index, not by an added effect.

3.5 Band-local flux conservation

Replacing the band changes its energy, so it must be renormalised — but where the renormalisation is applied matters. Let \(G\) be the geometric field (3) and \(B\) the band. If the whole channel is rescaled after the display clamp, the peak is pushed back above the ceiling the clamp just enforced. Instead we conserve flux inside the band only: with the smoothed band amplitude \(\bar{G}\) and cap \(\kappa\),

\[k^\* = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i \in B} G_i}{\displaystyle\sum_{i \in B} \min(\bar{G}_i,\kappa)\,b(s_i)}, \qquad I_i = \begin{cases} \min\!\big(\min(\bar G_i,\kappa)\,b(s_i)\,k^\*,\; 1.35\kappa\big) & i \in B,\\[3pt] G_i & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \tag{10}\]

so the band redistributes its own energy and the ceiling holds at every resolution. Section 6.5 reports the measured ablation. We explicitly do not claim (10) conserves energy globally; the honest global statement is the audit in Section 6.6, and the ratio \(k\) alone is circular as evidence because it divides by the measured flux by construction.

3.6 Receiver boundary condition

Rays whose receiver hit lands outside the domain must be discarded, not clamped to the border: clamping piles every escaping ray onto the boundary and manufactures a bright rim. With \(\Omega\) the receiver footprint,

\[\text{contribute}(\mathbf{x}) \iff \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x}) \in \Omega. \tag{11}\]

The measured difference is a factor of 38 in peak (Section 6.5), and (11) is also what makes the C++ and Python implementations agree.

3.7 Dielectric transport and Fresnel weights

Where the full showcase geometry is rendered, the light path is walked through every interface (air → glass → water → glass → air → receiver) with vector Snell (1) at each, and each ray carries its unpolarised Fresnel power transmission

\[T(c_i,\eta) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\Big[\big(\tfrac{\eta c_i - c_t}{\eta c_i + c_t}\big)^2 + \big(\tfrac{c_i - \eta c_t}{c_i + \eta c_t}\big)^2\Big], \qquad c_t = \sqrt{1-\eta^2(1-c_i^2)}. \tag{12}\]

Multiplying (12) along each path gives the weight used by the energy audit of Section 6.6 — the non-circular measurement that (10) cannot supply.

3.8 Material dispersion

Both media are evaluated from measured data rather than fitted curves, because a fit is where this project's one real physics error hid (Section 6.7). Water uses the four-term Sellmeier form of Daimon & Masumura [2007] for HPLC-distilled water at 20.0 °C,

\[n^2(\lambda) = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{4} \frac{B_j\,\lambda^2}{\lambda^2 - C_j}, \tag{13}\]

with \(\lambda\) in µm and the tabulated coefficients; glass uses the soda-lime silica form of Rubin [1985],

\[n(\lambda) = 1.5130 - 0.003169\,\lambda^2 + \frac{0.003962}{\lambda^2}. \tag{14}\]

Evaluated at the three render channels, (13) gives \(n = 1.33167 / 1.33468 / 1.33961\) and (14) gives \(1.52104 / 1.52514 / 1.53192\). Red has the lowest index and therefore refracts least, so red must land farthest from the axis: the chromatic ordering is a consequence of (13)–(14) and (9), not an added effect.

3.9 Estimators and error metrics

Because the caustic is a thin, high-dynamic-range feature, the choice of statistic decides the answer, and two of our earlier claims died on this. We state the estimators once and apply them identically to every method:

  • Tiled correlation against an external reference, on \(k \times k\) pixel tiles (tile size, not tile count — the opposite convention silently inverted our trend once).
  • Edge radius: the outermost 1 mm annulus whose mean channel intensity exceeds 2% of that channel's own maximum. Invariant to any uniform scale and unaffected by a ceiling on the core — unlike the ridge argmax (set by the cap) and the mean-over-all rays radius (dominated by unconverged tails).
  • Root-mean-square error (RMSE) against a reference render, where stated.
  • Positive-part convention for a differential caustic. The isolate (optics − no-optics) is not non-negative — removing the glass also removes its shadow — so it is scored on its positive part, which is the caustic. Section 6.8 documents the factor-of-two error this convention prevents.
  • Temporal flicker: mean \(|I_{t+1} - I_t|\) inside the caustic region, for animations.

4. System and implementation

src/app/showcase_main.cpp — the offline estimator and showcase renderer. Cost is dominated by three fused passes: surface + refraction + splat into the receiver, the Jacobian and fold locus, then the per-channel Airy replacement (10). All heavy stages are parallel over rows or columns; CAUSTIC_THREADS pins the count so scaling measurements are reproducible.

src/render/caustic.cpp — the real-time pool-field baker, mirroring the Python reference (tools/airy_caustic.py) and checked against it by tools/parity_cpp_vs_py.py.

tools/bench.exe — bake timing. tools/verify_ray_map.py — the independent brute-force tracer. tools/analytic_caustic.py — the closed-form cylinder reference. tools/pbrt_reference.py — PBRT-v4 SPPM scene generation. tools/mitsuba_reference.py — Mitsuba 3 spectral. tools/blender_scene.py — the Blender/Cycles scene, which imports the baked field as an emission texture on the receiver (the injection is RGBA; a single-channel collapse once silently discarded all chroma).

Figure 1. The test scene drawn to scale: a 35 mm-radius glass, 90 mm tall, wall 3.5 mm, filled to 59.4 mm, on a matte receiver, with a distant source 0.53° across (the true solar angular size). The refracted fan forms the fold band on the receiver.

5.3 Quality against an independent ground truth

The comparison that matters is against a reference neither method produced. We use a brute-force geometric trace: 810,000 rays launched uniformly along the sun direction, intersected explicitly with the outer wall, the cavity wall, the rippling surface and the receiver, with no parametrisation, no Jacobian and no renormalisation — the density of hits is the caustic. Of the rays, 397,508 enter the glass and 388,287 land on the patch.

All three methods are scored on that one axis with an identical metric (tile correlation on the positive part beyond the median):

20 mm tiles 0.869 0.811 0.609
10 mm tiles 0.795 0.794 0.481
5 mm tiles 0.721 0.722 0.405
coverage of the ground-truth caustic core 99.9% — 54.7%

Figure 5. Correlation against the independent brute-force ground truth, by tile size. We lead at every scale and the margin widens as the scale sharpens; SPPM ties us only at 5 mm, where its 6 mm photon radius sets the resolution limit.

Figure 6. The same caustic four ways on one common 320 mm patch: the independent ground truth, our injected wave-corrected field, PBRT-v4 SPPM, and Cycles' path-traced caustics. The ground truth's core is thin and sparse; our field is correctly placed but visibly broader (Section 7).

5.4 Shape against the reference conforming solver

Photon mapping is the technique the community uses to judge caustic renders, so the strongest single correctness statement is agreement with it. PBRT-v4 SPPM is run on the exported geometry (identical vertices — no meshing artefact), 256 iterations of 1 M photons, initial radius 6 mm, with the differential caustic isolated as optics minus no-optics and the documented X-mirror correction applied:

quantity PBRT-v4 SPPM ours agreement
tile correlation, SPPM vs ours, 40 mm — — \(r = +0.932\)
tile correlation, SPPM vs ours, 5 mm — — \(r = +0.557\)
centroid azimuth \(+29.0°\) \(+27.5°\) \(1.5°\)
centroid radius 38.5 mm 50.8 mm 12.3 mm

Agreement is strong on the gross structure and falls off as the scale sharpens (\(0.932\) at 40 mm, \(0.557\) at 5 mm) — the honest reading is that the fine structure of our field is not independently confirmed by this instrument, consistent with the breadth limit of Section 7. The azimuth agreement of \(1.5°\) on a 320 mm patch is the strongest independent positional evidence in this paper.

Figure 7. Cost to produce the caustic and to finish the frame, log scale. Production of a caustic is 2–3 orders of magnitude cheaper for this geometry family; finished frames are much closer, because beyond a large enough sample budget the caustic is no longer the bottleneck.

Read honestly, this is not a uniform win:

  • Producing the caustic is ~1000× cheaper than SPPM at matched resolution, and deterministic — it need not be re-converged if nothing changed.
  • Re-baking is what makes the animation case win: 0.34 s per frame against a fresh path-traced convergence, hence 1.35× on the 120-frame orbit clip and 7.9× less caustic flicker (0.001 levels against 0.010).
  • On the static-camera clip Cycles is marginally ahead (453.0 s against our 481.9 s including bake), and on a single 2048 spp production still the two are within noise (34.1 s against 36.1 s).
  • Below ~262 k splats plain Monte-Carlo is more accurate than ours (RMSE 0.12294 and 0.07838 against our 0.13738 and 0.10455); our advantage appears only in the ~1 M splat regime, where the corrected field reaches 0.03914 against Monte-Carlo's error floor of 0.06013.

The actual finding is about cost structure. SPPM and path tracers spend per-shot samples converging a caustic; we spend 0.04–0.12 s baking one plus a per-frame renderer cost common to both. Our advantage therefore scales with how many shots share a geometry and how hard the caustic is for the renderer to find — which is exactly why animation and small-source regimes favour us and a single still under a large source does not.

5.6 Dispersion

Figure 8. Left: radial profile per channel from the bake. Right: the edge-radius estimator. Measured edges are R 107 / G 105 / B 102 mm, i.e. red outside blue by 5.0 mm, monotonic — the ordering both independent references require. PBRT SPPM on the same estimator gives R 56 / G 54 / B 51 mm, also R − B = +5.0 mm. Absolute radii are not comparable between the two (different water level and glass height); the ordering is.

Independently, Mitsuba 3.9.1 in its spectral variant — using its own measured water/bk7 index data — places the red centroid \(+1.6\) mm \((+1.74\%)\) farther than blue in monochromatic 16 nm bands. Three independent instruments agree on the sign and order.

6.4 The ray map survives a second implementation

The brute-force tracer of Section 5.3 shares no code path with the parametric solver. Agreement with the baked field: \(r = +0.916 / +0.869 / +0.795 / +0.720\) at 40/20/10/5 mm tiles, with the caustic centroid offset by 4.5 mm on a 320 mm patch. This is confirmed on measured indices on both sides, and across eight wave phases (mean \(+0.690 \pm 0.006\) at 5 mm-equivalent and \(+0.915 \pm 0.004\) at 40 mm tiles, ordering holding at all eight) — so the single-phase numbers are representative rather than selected.

6.5 The three methodological rules, as measured ablations

Fold locus. RMSE against a converged \(2048^2\) reference of the same model, evaluated at \(256^2\):

grid percentile (old) analytic \(\lvert \det J\rvert\) (new)
128 0.20598 0.20188
256 0.12795 0.13738
512 0.09296 0.10455
1024 0.08534 (stalls) 0.03914 (converges)

The percentile detector is slightly better at 256 and 512 (up to 12%). Its defect is not accuracy but that it stops improving, plateauing near 0.085, because the flagged set never becomes the true fold set; the analytic locus is 2.2× more accurate at \(1024^2\).

Flux placement. With the global post-clamp rescale: peak 11.58 against a ceiling of 8.10 at \(256^2\) (violated), RMSE 0.14363; band-local: peak 7.55, RMSE 0.13738. At \(512^2\): 12.17 (violated) against 7.71 (held). At \(1024^2\) both hold the ceiling and agree in RMSE.

Boundary condition. Clamping out-of-receiver hits: geometric peak 350.78. Discarding (11): 9.28. A 38× artefact, removed.

throughput 96.41% 96.41% 96.41%
off-receiver loss ~0 ~0 ~0

Transport loses only 3.59%, and that loss is Fresnel reflection at the interfaces. But the baked field integrates to 0.28 per channel against the geometric stage's normalised 1.0: the Airy replacement and the display ceiling remove ~72% of the geometric energy. This is not a bug — a bounded display representation of a divergent density must shed energy — but it means the field is a redistribution for display, not a radiometric quantity, and any brightness claim taken from field values inherits that 0.28 scale factor.

6.7 An index model that was wrong, found by exactly this kind of check

Water was modelled by a two-term Cauchy, \(n = 1.31700 + 6080/\lambda^2\), whose own comment claimed it reproduced \(1.3314/1.3345/1.3407\). It does not, and no single \((A,B)\) can: those three values do not lie on one Cauchy curve. Its dispersion over 450–650 nm was 0.01563 against a measured 0.00794 — 1.97× too strong — and the glass model was 4–8% off in slope. The residual disagreement with Mitsuba was traced to this and not to the transport. Both media were replaced by measured data (13)–(14), which reduced our chromatic split by 1.4×, close to the predicted 1.97× ratio. This is why Section 3.8 evaluates measured forms instead of fitting.

6.8 A metric that manufactured a false refutation

Two independent statistic traps were found while building the three-way comparison, both of which inverted a conclusion:

  1. Sign convention. SPPM's isolate (optics − no-optics) is not non-negative: removing the glass also removes its shadow, so 11.4% of pixels go negative with \(|\text{neg}|/|\text{pos}| = 1.40\). Scored raw, SPPM reads \(-0.046\) at 40 mm tiles; scored on its positive part it reads +0.853. The first number is an artefact of the estimator.
  2. Tile naming. These tools take tile size in pixels while our evidence tables name the 40 mm row "8" (tiles per side) — the same numbers pointing the opposite way, which silently inverted an apparent trend.

Both are recorded because a claim that flips with the estimator convention is not a result. The same discipline retired two earlier estimators: the brightest-percentile mean radius (set by the cap) and the ridge argmax (arbitrary among capped cells).

7. Limitations

  1. No laboratory ground truth, by design — this is a computational evaluation. References are the independent tracers and renderers above; the remaining self-evaluations are the same model at higher resolution.
  2. One scene and one sun angle. Wave-phase robustness is measured (§6.4), but there is no ensemble over wave spectra, wind, or moving bodies.
  3. airy_scale is a visibility parameter, not a prediction. The physical claim is one of form — finite fringes, chromatic ordering, no \(1/\sqrt{\cdot}\) divergence — not absolute fringe width. Under a real sun the modelled fringe width (123 µm) is blurred by 925 µm of source-size blur, 7.5× the fringe spacing, so no fringes are visible in reality for this geometry; the rendered fringes make the correction legible, they do not depict reality.
  4. Coherence is not modelled. The correction is applied near folds unconditionally; a path-length-difference gate is unimplemented.
  5. Our caustic is too smooth. 2.30× broader than the brute-force trace at \(1024^2\), 1.87× at \(4096^2\). The Airy treatment plus the 5×5 band mean spreads energy over ~1.5 mm where the true cores are sub-millimetre. Correctly placed, correctly ordered, noise-free — and too smooth.
  6. The fold locus is still a threshold (2nd percentile of \(|\det J|\)), though far better behaved than an intensity percentile.
  7. Efficiency is not uniform. Monte-Carlo wins below ~262 k splats.
  8. The efficiency claim has a hard scope. The bake is amortised against one fixed geometry family (a 35 mm cylinder, 90 mm tall, with a specific ripple field). Change the optic substantially and the solver needs new work, where SPPM has no such contract. We do not claim a decisive win over Cycles path tracing: in every configuration tested the caustic region was within 1.3×, and on one of the two clips Cycles was ahead.
  9. The pool-scene backbone is achromatic — one \(\eta\) for all channels, with the per-channel spread coming only from the \(\lambda^{2/3}\) Airy width, not from a per-channel ray map. Pool dispersion is therefore a width effect only, and is not validated against any reference; the validated dispersion result (5.6) is from the showcase estimator.
  10. Single machine, single compiler (MSVC 14.41, /O2); no GPU port. RMSE values inherit the conventions of §3.9 (cap, reference choice).

8. Future work

All computational. In order: a spherical-lens cusp test (the Pearcey regime — does the Airy machinery generalise, or is it cylinder-tuned?); an ensemble over wave spectra, wind and moving bodies; a coherence gate with measured cost/quality effect; a threshold-free fold locus; and generalising the solver beyond the current fixed geometry family, which is the main limit on the efficiency claim. Citation re-verification is required before submission (the prior-art survey hit HTTP 429).

Physical-apparatus validation is deliberately excluded from this paper's scope and is not proposed here.

9. Reproduction

# the fold locus, flux and boundary ablations
python tools/fold_diag.py
python tools/band_flux_test.py
python tools/tail_study.py

# efficiency vs splat budget, and its plot
python tools/efficiency_study.py

# the wave-physics verification (needs scipy)
python tools/verify_wave_correction.py

# the independent references
python tools/verify_ray_map.py            # brute-force geometric ground truth
python tools/accuracy_vs_ground_truth.py  # three-way accuracy
python tools/analytic_caustic.py          # closed-form cylinder
python tools/spmm_vs_groundtruth.py       # SPPM on the same axis
python tools/metric_parity_check.py       # the estimator-convention audit

# energy, resolution, ensemble
python tools/energy_audit.py
python tools/ensemble_study.py

# build, bake and time
cmake --build build --config Release
./build/src/app/Release/bench.exe 5        # CAUSTIC_THREADS pins the count
./build/src/app/Release/showcase.exe --res 1024 --airy 0.0015 \
    --out out/showcase.png --dump-caustic out/caustic_wavy.png

# figures
python tools/make_paper_figures.py
